title: Starting a forest garden
subtitle: A layered growing system designed to need less work each year, not more.
excerpt: A forest garden is a layered growing system of trees, shrubs, perennial vegetables, and ground cover that functions like a woodland edge. Once established, it needs little cultivation and produces food from multiple layers each year.
sourceNotes: System design after Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (Green Books, 2010), the primary UK reference. Informed by Robert Hart's original work at Wenlock Edge and Patrick Whitefield's The Earth Care Manual (2004). Specific species hardiness and spacing cross-referenced with RHS plant data.

glossaryTerms.definition: A garden designed to mimic the structure of a woodland edge, with canopy trees, sub-canopy trees, shrubs, herbaceous perennials, ground cover, root crops, and climbers filling each layer. Produces food or useful materials from multiple layers with minimal cultivation.

A group of plants that benefit each other when grown together. In forest gardening, a guild typically includes a fruit tree surrounded by nitrogen-fixers, dynamic accumulators, ground cover, and pest-confusing aromatics.

content.text: is a growing system built in layers: canopy trees, sub-canopy trees and large shrubs, smaller shrubs, herbaceous perennials, ground cover, root crops, and climbers. Each layer uses a different slice of the available light and space. Established over five to ten years, a well-designed forest garden requires far less physical work per unit of food produced than an annual vegetable plot.

In temperate UK conditions, a forest garden is realistic in any plot from 50 square metres upwards. Small spaces favour lower canopy trees (apple on dwarfing rootstocks, damson, crab apple) rather than standard fruit trees. A forest garden starts slowly and rewards patience.

Assess the site before planting anything. Note where the sun falls through the day in winter (the worst case for light). Map the low points where cold air pools and late frosts settle. Identify prevailing wind directions and any existing structures that will provide shelter. Frost-tender plants go on the warmest, most sheltered spots; hardy species fill the exposed edges.

Plant the canopy layer in the first winter (November to February) while bare-root stock is available and cheapest. For a medium UK garden (200 to 500 square metres), this means two to four fruit trees on semi-dwarfing or dwarfing rootstocks. Space them to allow for their mature spread: 4 m apart for trees on M9 or M26 rootstock, 6 to 8 m for MM106.

Plant nitrogen-fixing companion trees or large shrubs alongside the fruit trees at this stage. Alder, sea buckthorn, and Siberian pea tree all fix nitrogen from the air and improve the soil around the canopy. Space companion trees 2 to 3 m from the nearest fruit tree.

attrs.title: Plant guilds around each tree
attrs.body: A plant guild surrounds each canopy tree with a supporting cast of plants. Around a fruit tree, plant comfrey (Bocking 14) for potassium-rich mulch, a nitrogen-fixer nearby, white clover or strawberry as ground cover, and borage or phacelia for pollinators. Guilds reduce work because the plants build their own fertility cycle.

content.text: Year 2: shrub layer and herbaceous perennials

By year two, the canopy trees are established. Add the shrub layer: currants, gooseberries, jostaberries, and elder fill the 1 to 2 m height band between the tree canopy and the ground. Plant them in the spaces between trees. Under and around the shrubs, plant herbaceous perennials: comfrey, perennial kale, lovage, sea kale, and ground-covering plants like alpine strawberry and good king henry.

around each canopy tree as the shrubs go in. The guild planting takes two to three seasons to fill in and begin functioning as a self-reinforcing unit. In the gap years, annual vegetables can occupy the open ground, provided they are removed before they shade the perennial layers.
Year 3 onwards: ground cover and management

Establish ground cover between and under the shrubs in year three. Ground elder (if the site already has it), white clover, wild garlic in shaded spots, and alpine strawberry all work well. The goal is no bare soil, which means fewer weeds, less moisture loss, and a habitat for ground beetles and other predatory insects.

From year five, a well-planted forest garden mostly manages itself. Tasks shift from cultivation to harvesting, selective pruning to manage light, and removing species that become too dominant. Introduce climbers (climbing roses, hops, runner beans in summer) onto any bare fence or wall space.

attrs.heading: Common early problems
attrs.intro: Most forest garden failures happen in the first three years.

items.cause: Competition from grass around the base, or the planting hole was too small.
items.fix: Mulch a 1 m circle around each tree base with woodchip or straw in spring. Keep the circle clear of competing vegetation for the first three seasons. Do not fertilise in the first year; let the roots grow into the native soil.

items.cause: Sea buckthorn and alder both need well-drained soil; they rot in waterlogged ground.
items.fix: Improve drainage at the planting point. Raise on a small mound if the soil is clay-heavy. Siberian pea tree tolerates wetter conditions than sea buckthorn.

items.symptom: Annual weeds taking over the open ground in years 1 and 2
items.cause: Normal in the establishment phase; the perennial layer has not yet closed the canopy.
items.fix: Hoe the open ground between plants. Sow a temporary green manure (phacelia or white clover) over bare soil to occupy it and add fertility while the perennials establish.
